notes: Interim injunction on CTRL NEC project manager impartiality; serious issues found but injunction refused.

enrichment.short_title: Costain v Bechtel: project manager impartiality on CTRL contract C105

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: CORBER, a consortium including Costain, carried out St Pancras CTRL works under NEC-based contract C105 with employer URN and project manager RLE, dominated by Bechtel.
After payment certificate 48 disallowed substantially more costs, CORBER alleged Mr Bassily instructed Bechtel staff at an April 2005 meeting to assess payments partially in Bechtel's interests.
CORBER sought interim injunctions requiring impartial assessment and certification; Bechtel and Mr Bassily denied bad faith and contended RLE owed no duty of impartiality.
Payment disputes were subject to contract adjudication and arbitration procedures under section 9 of the contract.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim injunction application in TCC proceedings alleging Bechtel and Mr Bassily procured URN's breach of contract C105.
enrichment.outcome: CORBER passed the American Cyanamid threshold on serious issues to be tried but the interim injunction application was refused on balance of convenience.
enrichment.ratio: It is at least arguable that when assessing sums payable under contract C105 the project manager must act impartially as between employer and contractor, following Sutcliffe v Thackrah; nevertheless interim injunctions are inappropriate where elaborate contractual dispute resolution and damages provide adequate remedies.
legal_issues: What Mr Bassily instructed Bechtel staff to do at the 15 April 2005 meeting
Whether RLE's duty when assessing payments was impartiality or acting in the employer's interests
Whether RLE breached that duty and URN was thereby in breach of contract
Whether Bechtel and Mr Bassily procured breach of contract and whether interim relief should be granted
linked_authorities: Sutcliffe v Thackrah [1974] AC 727
American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396
Royal Brompton Hospital NHS Trust v Hammond (No 8) [2002] EWHC 2037 (TCC)

confidence.notes: Six identified issues and final refusal of interim relief are clearly reasoned though URN was not a party.

notes: Cargo claim service extensions upheld despite claimant delay; Gartner aware of proceedings throughout.

enrichment.short_title: P&G v Gartner: extension of time to serve cargo claim in Austria
key_facts: P&G claimed about €300,000 for Pampers lost from the MV Sybille on a shipment from Spain to Manchester in January 2003.
Proceedings were issued on 30 April 2004 against Austrian carrier Gartner but not promptly served out of the jurisdiction.
Two without-notice extensions to 31 May 2005 were granted; Gartner applied to set them aside on inadequate explanation of delay.
Gartner had been negotiating with recovery agents, knew proceedings had been issued, and did not oppose the first extension.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Rehearing of Gartner's application to set aside orders extending time for service of the claim form out of the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Gartner's application refused; the extensions of time for service were upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Although P&G's explanations for delay in serving were thin and did not fully comply with the Practice Direction, refusing extensions would be disproportionate where the defendant knew of the claim, had not been prejudiced, and delay largely reflected settlement negotiations and foreign service requirements.
legal_issues: Whether P&G gave a sufficient explanation for failing to serve within the original time limit
Whether the court should exercise its discretion to set aside the two extensions
Whether delay was disproportionate given Gartner's awareness of the claim and lack of prejudice
Whether a time-bar defence would have been available if fresh proceedings were brought
linked_authorities: Hashtroodi v Hancock [2004] EWCA Civ 652

confidence.notes: Discretionary outcome and Hashtroodi calibration analysis are explicit though some delay periods were poorly explained.

notes: Adjudication enforcement with stay refused; Order 47 principles comprehensively restated.

enrichment.short_title: Wimbledon Construction v Vago: stay of adjudication enforcement refused

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Wimbledon Construction carried out extension works at Mr Vago's home under a JCT Minor Works contract with adjudication provisions.
Adjudicator Mr Judkins awarded £122,923.34; Vago consented to judgment but sought a stay pending arbitration citing the claimant's uncertain finances.
The claimant also sought summary judgment for £6,507.97 for agreed post-contract works; Vago's vague defects counterclaim was rejected.
Accountants described the company as technically insolvent at May 2004 but modest profit was shown by May 2005 and financial difficulties were linked to non-payment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Enforcement proceedings for an adjudicator's decision with applications for summary judgment and stay of execution under RSC Order 47.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment granted for £129,431.31 inclusive of VAT; stay of execution refused.
enrichment.ratio: Adjudicators' decisions should be enforced summarily and a stay under Order 47 requires special circumstances such as probable inability to repay; where the claimant's financial position was unchanged since contract and largely caused by the defendant's non-payment, stay is inappropriate.
legal_issues: Whether summary judgment should be granted for post-contract works despite a defects counterclaim
Whether special circumstances under Order 47 justified staying enforcement of the adjudication award
Whether the claimant probably could not repay the judgment sum after arbitration
The interaction between adjudication enforcement and RSC Order 47 principles
linked_authorities: Bouygues UK Ltd v Dahl-Jensen UK Ltd [2000] BLR 522
Herschell Engineering Ltd v Breen Property Ltd (unreported, 28 July 2000)
AWG Construction Services Ltd v Rockingham Motor Speedway [2004] EWHC 888 (TCC)

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on financial position and comprehensive statement of applicable principles.

notes: Linked patent actions; summary judgment on novelty and Swiss-type claims refused.

enrichment.short_title: Tercica v Genentech: summary judgment refused on IGF-I patent revocation
key_facts: Tercica, a licensee, sued Avecia and Insmed for infringement of a Genentech patent on combined IGF-I and IGFBP-3 for producing an anabolic state by subcutaneous bolus injection.
Avecia and Insmed cross-claimed for revocation, concentrating on novelty over Binkert, Spencer II and Maack and section 4(2) method-of-treatment arguments.
Claim 1 concerned use of IGF-I and BP-3 in specified molar ratios; construction of 'anabolic state' was disputed.
Expert evidence on skilled person construction and prior art disclosure was extensive but inconclusive at summary stage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Summary judgment applications in linked infringement and revocation actions concerning a Swiss-type second medical use patent.
enrichment.outcome: Applications for summary judgment and striking out dismissed; revocation and infringement claims to proceed to trial.
enrichment.ratio: Patent construction requiring the mantle of the skilled person and disputed prior art disclosures are rarely suitable for summary determination; applicants failed to show Genentech had no real prospect of defending novelty where 'anabolic state' construction and General Tire flag-planting issues remained genuinely arguable.
legal_issues: Construction of 'producing an anabolic state' in claim 1 and whether Maack anticipated
Whether Binkert and Spencer II disclosed the IGF-I/BP-3 combination and therapeutic use with sufficient clarity
Whether molar ratio and bolus injection features confer novelty on a Swiss-type claim
Whether the patent claims a method of treatment excluded by section 4(2)
linked_authorities: Celador Productions Ltd v Melville [2004] EWHC 2362 (Ch)
Monsanto Co v Merck & Co Inc [2000] RPC 77
General Tire & Rubber Co v Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co Ltd [1972] RPC 457

confidence.notes: Summary judgment refusal and construction/previous art reasoning are detailed though final patent validity remains undetermined.

notes: Forced antipsychotic treatment challenge dismissed after HL reversed classification restriction.

enrichment.short_title: R(B) v Haddock: compulsory medication under the Mental Health Act
key_facts: B, detained at Ashworth since age 18 under section 37/41 orders, challenged forcible depot antipsychotic medication commenced in May 2004.
Independent experts Professor Sashidharan and Professor McGuire argued he had no mental disorder and was a case of psychiatric injustice.
A SOAD certificate under section 58(3)(b) was granted in October 2004 after an earlier certificate was withdrawn during proceedings.
Previous medication periods had shown some behavioural improvement; B lacked capacity to refuse treatment and resisted cooperation with staff.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of treatment under Part IV of the Mental Health Act 1983 with full merits review following Wilkinson and R(N).
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; compulsory antipsychotic treatment was convincingly shown to be medically necessary.
enrichment.ratio: On a Wilkinson merits review the court must decide whether treatment is convincingly medically necessary under Herczegfalvy; where a patient lacks capacity and prior medication alleviated his condition, the RMO and SOAD views should not readily be overruled, and post-HL classification is not decisive to permissibility of treatment.
legal_issues: Whether B was suffering from mental disorder justifying detention and treatment
Whether B had capacity to refuse consent under section 58
Whether depot antipsychotic medication was necessary and likely to alleviate his condition
Whether treatment breached Articles 3 and 8 ECHR and the role of SOAD certification
linked_authorities: R(Wilkinson) v Broadmoor Special Hospital Authority [2002] 1 WLR 419
R(B) v Ashworth Hospital Authority [2005] 2 WLR 695

confidence.notes: Extensive medical history and application of Wilkinson/Herczegfalvy test are clearly recorded.

notes: Liability trial; 10% commission claim rejected and Waitrose bonus held unenforceable.

enrichment.short_title: Assi v Dina Foods: unpaid commission and bonus claims rejected
key_facts: Mr Assi worked part-time as national sales manager for Dina Foods from December 1997, paid £5.77 per hour while claiming Jobseeker's Allowance.
He claimed an oral agreement for 10% commission on all sales and a £4,000 bonus promised after securing a Waitrose deal in 2000.
Contemporaneous employment records, payslips and benefits correspondence made no reference to commission; he signed a full and final settlement in November 2000.
The claimant drafted witness statements for others in identical language and was found likely to have attempted to bribe a witness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on liability only before Master Eyre's order, following claims for unpaid commission of about £192,000 and a £4,000 bonus.
enrichment.outcome: Commission claim failed entirely; although a £4,000 Waitrose bonus promise was found on the balance of probabilities, it was unenforceable for lack of consideration.
enrichment.ratio: Where contemporaneous documents and employment records consistently show hourly pay only, an alleged oral commission agreement is improbable and unsupported; a gratuitous promise made after a deal is concluded lacks consideration and is not saved by Williams v Roffey Bros.
legal_issues: Whether an oral agreement to pay 10% commission on sales was made in October 1997
Whether contemporaneous documents and Jobseeker's Allowance arrangements contradicted the commission claim
Whether Mr Haddad promised a £4,000 bonus after the Waitrose deal
Whether the bonus promise was enforceable for want of consideration
linked_authorities: Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd [1991] 1 QB 1
Stilk v Myrick (1809) 2 Camp 317

confidence.notes: Detailed factual findings on documents, credibility and bonus law are comprehensive.

notes: Solicitor negligence damages; income-stream loss preferred over diminution in value.

enrichment.short_title: Keydon v Eversheds: measure of damages for negligent lease advice
key_facts: Keydon, advised by Eversheds, bought the freehold reversion of Willow House Cardiff as a secure income investment in April 2002.
Eversheds negligently advised that a sub-lease to Hyder did not assign the head lease, leaving WPD liable on covenants.
Hyder entered administration in December 2002; WPD successfully argued in arbitration that it was released from rent obligations.
Diminution in value was agreed at £110,000 but historical rent losses alone substantially exceeded that figure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on measure of damages after Eversheds admitted negligence in advising on the effect of a sub-lease under the 1997 head lease.
enrichment.outcome: Claim broadly succeeded; diminution in value rule rejected and damages assessed by reference to lost alternative income stream to judgment date.
enrichment.ratio: Where a solicitor knows property is bought for investment income, diminution in value may undercompensate; damages may be measured by the income stream the client would have obtained from an alternative investment had correct advice been given, applying SAAMCO and East v Maurer principles.
legal_issues: Whether the diminution in value rule or an income-stream approach should measure Keydon's loss
What alternative investment Keydon would have made but for negligent advice
Whether comparable commercial properties were available in April 2002
The appropriate rent review figure, dilapidations loss and future rent void periods
linked_authorities: South Australia Asset Management Corp v York Montague Ltd [1997] AC 191
East v Maurer [1991] 1 WLR 461
Greymalkin Ltd v Copleys (a firm) [2004] PNLR 44

confidence.notes: Measure of damages reasoning is detailed though dilapidations figure requires further inquiry.

notes: Planning enforcement appeal; no alternative site defence rejected under section 179(3).

enrichment.short_title: Wycombe v Wells: section 179 enforcement notice defence rejected
key_facts: Mr Wells, a gypsy, was prosecuted for failing to comply with an enforcement notice requiring cessation of use of Ashbrook Farm as a caravan site.
Magistrates acquitted him holding he had done all he reasonably could to find alternative accommodation given a local gypsy site shortage.
Wells had not applied to the housing authority after the enforcement notice; selling his mobile home would only fund about ten months' rent.
His children attended local schools and planning issues including accommodation shortage had already been considered on appeal against the notice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' acquittal on a prosecution under section 179(2) of the 1990 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the section 179(3) defence was not made out in law and the question was answered 'No'.
enrichment.ratio: Section 179(3) requires the owner to show he did everything reasonably expected to secure compliance with the notice, not merely that no alternative site was available; inability to find another site where the activity could continue does not establish the statutory defence where the owner had power and resources to leave the land.
legal_issues: Whether inability to find alternative gypsy accommodation constitutes a section 179(3) defence
Whether personal or financial hardship excuses non-compliance with an enforcement notice
The correct construction of 'did everything he could be expected to do to secure compliance'
Whether planning merits and homelessness issues can be re-litigated in enforcement prosecutions
linked_authorities: R v Beard [1997] 1 PLR 64
Kent County Council v Brockman (1996) 1 PLR 1
R v Thomas George Clarke [2002] EWCA Crim 753

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and distinction from Beard and Brockman are clearly reasoned.

notes: Drink-driving appeal dismissed; pre-test conversation held not a PACE interview.

enrichment.short_title: Ridehalgh v DPP: PACE Code C and excess alcohol prosecution
key_facts: Inspector Hodnett, a British Transport Police officer, smelled alcohol on PC Ridehalgh at Crawley police station in April 2004.
Before a breath test, Ridehalgh admitted drinking the previous night and driving to the station that morning.
A positive screening test led to arrest, caution and repeat admissions under caution with further detail.
Magistrates found the pre-test conversation was preliminary questioning analogous to a roadside stop, not an interview requiring caution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated against conviction for driving with excess alcohol contrary to section 5(1)(a) of the 1988 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no breach of PACE Code C and conviction inevitable in any event given subsequent cautioned admissions.
enrichment.ratio: A caution under Code C paragraph 10.1 is required only when there are grounds to suspect an offence; preliminary questions about driving and drinking before grounds exist do not constitute an interview, following Whelehan v DPP; subsequent admissions under caution render any earlier breach immaterial.
legal_issues: Whether the pre-breath-test conversation was an interview requiring caution under Code C
Whether grounds to suspect drink-driving existed before the screening test
Whether a Code C breach tainted subsequent cautioned admissions
Whether Batley v Hampshire Justices or Whelehan v DPP governed the facts
linked_authorities: Whelehan v Director of Public Prosecutions [1995] RTR 177
Batley v Hampshire Justices [1998] EWHC Admin 212

confidence.notes: Magistrates' findings and Code C construction are clearly applied to the specific facts.

notes: Pharmacy Act erasure appeal dismissed; sustained threatening conduct against Unichem directors.

enrichment.short_title: Chanin v RPS: erasure upheld for threatening conduct against Unichem
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Chanin, pharmacist directors of Chanins Pharmacy Ltd, defaulted on an £850,000 Unichem refinancing agreement leading to receivership in April 2002.
Over more than a year they sent threatening letters, grim reaper imagery, harassing calls and published directors' personal details on mock websites.
Their adviser Mr Jones also threatened Unichem officers and contacted directors' wives; the Chanins were subject to a High Court injunction.
The statutory committee found professional misconduct proved and directed erasure for lack of insight; misconduct was no longer contested on appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 10 of the Pharmacy Act 1954 against erasure from the Register following Royal Pharmaceutical Society disciplinary proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; erasure was proportionate and no lesser penalty appropriate.
enrichment.ratio: Pharmacists must conduct business dealings with integrity and must not engage in sustained offensive and threatening conduct likely to bring the profession into disrepute; where there is a remarkable lack of insight and conduct was integral to business disputes, erasure is appropriate despite previous good character.
legal_issues: Whether erasure was disproportionate to the misconduct found
Whether conduct was extraneous to professional practice as pharmacists
Whether the committee exaggerated the seriousness of the allegations
Whether responsibility for Mr Jones's conduct was wrongly attributed to the appellants

confidence.notes: Penalty-only appeal with detailed committee findings and clear lack-of-insight reasoning.
